doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Writing arrangements for the Mississippians and bebop in 1945
summary: He wrote dance arrangements for the Ole Miss band and recalls hearing Salt Peanuts; Audre notes his Lester Young and Dizzy taste.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Where I’m gradually heading with this is how music progressed from being a kind of hobby to your life’s work.
I don’t know.
We’ll get there.
Well, I wrote arrangements for the Mississippi band, and...
Before you entered the army, or after?
Yeah, I think so—before I went. I don’t know. It was later. I remember writing arrangements for the Mississippians.
Yeah. They still use some of them.
Dance arrangements?
Yes.
When you wrote those arrangements, were they informed by listening to dance...hot bands?
Well, they were listening to bebop!
Yeah!
Wow. So those records made it down to Mississippi before you went into the Army.
Yeah...I think so.
I’ll name a couple of records. Tell me if you heard them. “The Jumping Blues,” Jay McShann...
No, Jay McShann I made later.
How about “Salt Peanuts”? That was recorded in 1945. That’s why I’m asking.
Oh, yeah, I remember “Salt Peanuts.”
“Red Cross,” which Charlie Parker made in 1944.
I don’t know.
When I met you, you liked Lester Young and Dizzy Gillespie. There were a lot of people you liked then.
Yeah, well...
Well, by then it was 1950...
‘49. [LAUGHS]
